analysis.one_liner: Reopens court filing deadlines for people injured by atomic weapons testing so they can sue over their losses.
analysis.headline: Harry Reid's bill to reopen nuclear-weapons-testing injury lawsuits died in a Senate subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed a provision in the 1991 defense authorization law (Section 3141) that governed who could be sued for injuries, deaths, and property losses tied to atomic weapons testing, and replaced it with rules friendlier to people filing those claims. It also would have stopped the clock on filing deadlines from 1984 until the bill became law, letting people whose lawsuits were dismissed or whose deadlines expired start over — with a one-year window to refile. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never came up again before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who lived downwind of or worked on atomic weapons test sites — and their families — who suffered injury, death, or property loss and lost their day in court because a deadline passed or a case was dismissed under the 1984 and 1990 provisions. Their claims would be revived and they would have had one year to file again.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 3141 of the Fiscal Year 1991 defense authorization act, which governed civil actions over injury, death, or property loss arising from atomic weapons testing programs.

Stops the clock on federal and state filing deadlines for these claims from October 19, 1984 (when a 1984 law first barred many of them) until enactment, so claims dismissed or time-barred during that period could be brought again.
Specifically revives lawsuits that were filed before October 19, 1984 and later dismissed under those provisions, letting them be recommenced.
Gives any otherwise-expiring claim a final one-year window to be filed after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, on behalf of taxpayers, would bear judgments or settlements in revived lawsuits, and the defense contractors that ran the weapons test sites would face renewed litigation exposure. The government had inserted itself into these claims partly to shield those contractors.

drawbacks.text: Reviving claims that may be decades old is expensive for the federal treasury, and old cases are harder to defend fairly because memories fade, witnesses die, and records disappear.

The 1990 provision had channeled these suits against the United States rather than the contractors who actually ran the test sites; repealing it reopens questions about who ultimately pays for injuries caused by secret government work performed under contract.

Because the bill never advanced, its practical design was never tested in committee — for example, whether a blanket deadline restart was the fairest way to separate viable claims from stale ones was never examined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the affected downwinders, test-site workers, and their families, the stakes were concrete: access to court for injuries from nuclear weapons testing, many of which were fatal cancers and lost property. The main cost falls on taxpayers through the federal treasury and on the litigation system in handling old cases. The tolling approach — a flat clock-stop from 1984 onward plus a one-year refiling window — is a blunt instrument, and it was never refined because the bill never received a hearing. On balance, the bill's benefits went to a defined group of injured people while its costs were diffuse; the honest weakness is that reviving very old claims carries real evidentiary and fiscal costs that the bill's one-year window only partly addresses.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and then to its courts subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Harry Reid of Nevada introduced the bill on October 17, 1991, for himself and Senator Bryan, both representing the state that hosted the Nevada Test Site.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
Six days later it was referred further to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts and Administrative Practice.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors that ran the atomic weapons test sites and the federal government came out ahead: the 1990 provision limiting these lawsuits stayed on the books, and people whose claims had been dismissed or time-barred never got their day in court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors and the federal government

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the atomic-weapons-testing contractor liability provision and revive dismissed or time-barred claims.

for.name: Richard Bryan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside Senator Reid.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — never reported the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, passed it to the Subcommittee on Courts and Administrative Practice, and never held a hearing or voted it out.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded support was its two Democratic sponsors from Nevada, and no member is recorded as opposing it.

industries.industry: Defense contractors operating nuclear weapons test sites
industries.note: Federal law had stepped in to route atomic-testing injury claims against the United States, shielding the contractors that actually ran the test sites from being sued. This bill would have peeled back that protection and revived old claims, so the contractors' interest lay in the bill going nowhere — which is what happened.
The United States had been substituted as the defendant in these claims, so revived lawsuits would mean payouts from the treasury — the flip side of restoring a legal remedy for injured citizens.
